intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that Noonan syndrome-like disorder with loose anagen hair-1 (NSLH1) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the SHOC2 gene (602775) on chromosome 10q25.2.

paragraphs.text: Noonan syndrome-like disorder with loose anagen hair combines features resembling Noonan syndrome with distinctive ectodermal abnormalities. Mazzanti et al. (2003) and Cordeddu et al. (2009) described short stature, often with growth hormone (GH) deficiency, macrocephaly, cognitive deficits with hyperactive behavior, a hypernasal voice, and cardiac anomalies. The hair is easily pluckable, sparse, thin and slow-growing (loose anagen hair), and the skin is darkly pigmented, often with eczema or ichthyosis. Cordeddu et al. (2009) found that mitral valve dysplasia and septal defects were overrepresented compared with the general Noonan syndrome population.

paragraphs.text: Mazzanti et al. (2003) described 3 children with the same facial phenotype, which was not completely typical of Noonan syndrome. All 3 had short stature, macrocephaly, enlarged cerebrospinal fluid spaces, a short neck with redundant skin, severe GH deficiency, and mild psychomotor delay with attention deficit-hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). Two had mild dilatation of the pulmonary root. They also shared a unique combination of ectodermal abnormalities: darkly pigmented, hairless skin and hair defined as loose anagen hair. The authors felt that this combination, together with the behavioral phenotype and GH deficiency, fit no known condition.

paragraphs.text: Cordeddu et al. (2009) reviewed 25 individuals with a SHOC2 mutation and found a consistent phenotype. Facial features appeared typical of Noonan syndrome. Common features included macrocephaly, high forehead, hypertelorism, palpebral ptosis, low-set, posteriorly rotated ears, a short, webbed neck, and pectus anomalies. Growth was reduced, often with proven GH deficiency. Patients had cognitive deficits and a distinctive hyperactive behavior that improved with age in most. The hair was easily pluckable, sparse, thin and slow-growing, and in 12 subjects loose anagen hair was confirmed by microscopic examination of pulled hairs. Most patients had darkly pigmented skin with eczema or ichthyosis, and the voice was characteristically hypernasal. Most had cardiac anomalies; mitral valve dysplasia and septal defects were significantly overrepresented compared with the general Noonan syndrome population. Referring pediatricians had felt that several patients had features suggestive of Costello syndrome or cardiofaciocutaneous syndrome as newborns or young infants.

paragraphs.text: Hoban et al. (2012) reported a male infant with a de novo SHOC2 p.Ser2Gly mutation. Fetal distress required premature delivery at 32 weeks. After birth he had dysmorphic features, edema, hepatosplenomegaly, leukocytosis, thrombocytopenia, and respiratory distress. Echocardiography showed hypertrophic cardiomyopathy with left ventricular outflow tract obstruction. The cardiac lesion progressed rapidly, and he was discharged home for palliative care. The authors noted that his cardiac findings and features were not typical of previously reported patients with this mutation.

paragraphs.text: Gripp et al. (2013) reported 5 males with the SHOC2 p.Ser2Gly mutation. Four of them (Patients 1, 2, 3 and 5) had been suspected of having Costello syndrome. All 5 had skin hyperpigmentation, sparse light-colored hair, increased fine wrinkles, ligamentous laxity, and developmental delay. All 4 who were assessed had a structural cardiac anomaly. Hypotonia and macrocephaly occurred in 4 of 5. Three of 5 had polyhydramnios, increased birth weight, or required a feeding tube. None had been formally diagnosed with loose anagen hair by microscopy. All had sparse, very slow-growing hair of unruly texture and unusually light color, together with unusually long eyelashes. Patient 5 never had hair loss or easily pluckable hair.

paragraphs.text: Brain imaging in the Gripp et al. (2013) series showed relative megalencephaly with enlarged subarachnoid spaces, which the authors considered most consistent with benign external hydrocephalus. All 4 patients assessed had a relatively small posterior fossa, indicated by a vertical tentorium. The authors suggested that this combination accounted for the high rate of cerebellar tonsillar ectopia. Patient 4, a boy of Mexican ancestry, had mild ventriculomegaly and periventricular nodular heterotopia. By age 6 years he had developed a Chiari I malformation, in the context of platybasia, basilar invagination, and fusion of the C3 and C4 vertebrae. He also had an atrial septal defect, severe eczema, and blond, easily pluckable hair that was much lighter than his family's. Including literature cases, 3 of 8 patients with MRI had a Chiari I malformation.

paragraphs.text: Cordeddu et al. (2009) found the heterozygous SHOC2 mutation in sporadic patients with Noonan syndrome-like disorder with loose anagen hair-1 and showed it to be de novo in all families with parental DNA available. The paper calls the phenotype 'Noonan syndrome', but p.Ser2Gly is the mutation that defines OMIM's Noonan syndrome-like disorder with loose anagen hair-1, so the draft's disease name is standard nomenclature for the same condition. paragraphs.text: Cordeddu et al. (2009) used an in silico protein network analysis, seeded with known RAS-MAPK disease proteins, to rank candidate genes for Noonan syndrome. They resequenced the top candidate, SHOC2, in 96 Noonan syndrome patients without mutations in known genes. Four unrelated sporadic individuals carried a heterozygous c.4A-G transition predicting a ser2-to-gly (S2G) substitution. In 3 of these, parental DNA was available; the change was absent in both parents and paternity was confirmed. The mutation was present in DNA from several tissues, which indicated germline origin. Among 410 further mutation-negative subjects with Noonan syndrome or a related phenotype, 21 had the same change, and it was de novo in all 12 families with parental DNA available. No other disease-associated SHOC2 variant was found. In Cos-1 cells, the S2G mutant took up [3H]-myristic acid, whereas wildtype SHOC2 and a disease-unrelated S2A mutant did not. The S2G mutant was targeted to the cell membrane and did not move to the nucleus after EGF stimulation. In Neuro2A cells it increased EGF-dependent ERK phosphorylation.

paragraphs.text: Hannig et al. (2014) identified a heterozygous SHOC2 c.519G-A (M173I) variant in a 5-year-old girl of European ancestry and her father. paragraphs.text: Cordeddu et al. (2009) found a heterozygous c.4A-G transition in the SHOC2 gene, predicting a ser2-to-gly (S2G) substitution, in 25 individuals with Noonan syndrome-like disorder with loose anagen hair (NSLH1). Where parental DNA was available, the mutation was de novo: in 3 of 4 individuals in the first cohort and in 12 families in the second. No other disease-associated SHOC2 variant was found. The substitution creates an N-myristoylation site. The mutant protein took up [3H]-myristic acid, was targeted to the plasma membrane, did not translocate to the nucleus after EGF stimulation, and increased EGF-dependent ERK phosphorylation in Neuro2A cells.
